items.title: Roger Kellaway interviewed by Monk Rowe, Los Angeles, California, February 14, 1999
items.q: there’s too much Webern and Alban Berg and Prokofiev and Stravinsky, and onward to Stockhausen and Messiaen and more modern composers that have shaped my thinking about what sound is about

ctx.x: Okay. So improvising to you is not necessarily only a jazz — in the jazz idiom.

That’s right. And the reason that I decided on that particular category for myself is because the idea of what a jazz pianist does is too limiting. I’ve listened to much too much twentieth century classical music, which is the necessary ingredient for your understanding how it is I play and how I think, for me to just think of myself as a jazz pianist, because there’s too much Webern and Alban Berg and Prokofiev and Stravinsky, and onward to Stockhausen and Messiaen and more modern composers that have shaped my…

When you play, for instance I’ll use last night as an example, I heard you play “All Blues.” It was very interesting because we weren’t sure what the tune was going to be, and you started playing, you and Bob Magnusson just basically started playing. Do you have an idea before your hands hit the keyboard, as where that’s going, that introduction?
